name: DHT / Androgel for facial structure

card.summary: Topical DHT or testosterone gel pitched in forums for masculinising the face during puberty; gels are studied for low testosterone in older men, not for facial structure.
card.note: Pharmaceutical DHT is not available in the US or Canada; forum use often involves unregulated or homemade products. Trials have been in older men, not adolescents.

quick.overview:
Topical DHT (dihydrotestosterone) gel is promoted by some looksmaxxing posters as a way to enhance brow ridge, jaw and cheek development, especially in puberty. AndroGel is a brand of testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism, and discussion sometimes uses it alongside or instead of DHT gel.

The human trials found concern older men with low testosterone, looking at well-being, sexual function, cognition and the prostate. None tested facial bone structure or adolescents.
quick.mechanism: DHT is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase and acts locally in tissues. It is linked to facial and body hair, prostate growth and male genital development. Forum proponents argue it drives facial dimorphism, but published studies have not tested that.
quick.risks: Testosterone gels can transfer to others by contact and are reported to raise prostate-specific antigen modestly. A trial in healthy men found DHT administration did not raise intraprostatic androgen concentrations. Pharmaceutical DHT is unavailable in the US and Canada.

lead: DHT gel and AndroGel for facial structure is a hormonal protocol discussed on looksmaxxing forums. Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is an androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in target tissues, and it acts mainly locally. It is associated with facial and body hair, prostate and genital development.[1] AndroGel is a testosterone gel approved for male hypogonadism.[2]

As a medication, DHT is called androstanolone and is sold in forms including topical gels in certain European countries, but it is not available in the US or Canada.[1] Trials of DHT gel have been conducted in older men with symptoms of low testosterone.[3][4] No study has tested DHT or testosterone gel for facial bone development.
infobox: Not in US or Canada; some European countries[1]

paras: Transdermal testosterone gels were introduced in the US in 2000 and reach steady-state testosterone levels within about 24 hours of application, with a profile comparable to patches and without the peaks and troughs of injectable esters.[2] Pharmaceutical DHT (androstanolone, brand Andractim) is available in tablets, gels and injectable esters in some European countries.[1]

DHT is made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase and circulates at about one-tenth the level of testosterone. DHT is linked to facial and body hair growth and pattern hair loss, while testosterone is linked to musculoskeletal development, voice deepening and libido. People with 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency develop reduced facial and body hair but still show voice deepening and musculoskeletal changes at puberty.[1]

Reviews of testosterone gel report that application-site reactions occur less than with patches and polycythaemia risk is lower than with injections.[2] The risk of secondary exposure through skin contact is a recognised challenge for gels.[5]
No studies found on topical DHT or testosterone gel for facial structure or in adolescents for appearance. Related studies concern other populations.

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 120 men aged 50 to 70 examined DHT gel for general well-being, sexual function and the prostate.[3] A registered Phase 2 study tested DHT gel for symptoms of low testosterone in men aged 55 to 80.[4] A randomised trial in healthy men found that DHT administration did not increase intraprostatic androgen concentrations.[6] A long-term study of AndroGel in hypogonadal men for up to 42 months reported sustained effects on sexual function, mood, lean and fat mass and bone mineral density.[7]

A long looksmax.org post argues that topical DHT applied during puberty could enhance the development of the brow ridge, jawline and cheekbones, describing DHT as more androgenic than testosterone and non-aromatising, and saying the topic is often mocked on the forum.[8] Other threads on the forum ask about the effects of facial application and use for mandible growth.[9]

timeline.event: Transdermal testosterone gels introduced in the US.[2]
A randomised placebo-controlled trial of transdermal DHT in aging men is published.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, DHT gel threads propose it as a puberty-stage tool for facial masculinisation, and other members dispute or joke about the idea.[8]

claims.claim: Topical DHT during puberty enhances masculine facial bone development.
claims.believers: A long post says DHT is the main driver of secondary male traits such as brow ridge, jawline and cheekbones and that optimising androgen receptors in these areas during development would increase masculinity.[8]
claims.experts: No published studies have tested DHT gel for facial bone development. Medical sources link DHT to hair growth and prostate and genital development.[1]

claims.claim: DHT gel is among the safest looksmaxxing tools.
claims.believers: The same post describes DHT gel as the best and safest tool outside height maximisation for those in puberty.[8]
claims.experts: In a trial in healthy men, DHT did not raise intraprostatic androgen concentrations.[6]
